content: Batyr was an Asian elephant born in 1970 and lived his entire life in the Karaganda Zoo in Kazakhstan. He passed away in the spring of 1993. Remarkably, Batyr never encountered another elephant during his lifetime. He was the offspring of Indian elephants, a subspecies of the Asian elephant, named Palm (his mother) and Dubas (his father). These elephants were originally gifted to Kazakhstan's Almaty Zoo by Indian Prime Minister Jawaharlal Nehru. Batyr's name, derived from a Turkic word, translates to The Dashing Equestrian, The Man of Courage, or The Athlete. Batyr first demonstrated his extraordinary ability to mimic human speech in the winter of 1977, just before New Year's Day. Zoo employees were the first to notice his vocalizations, which included asking for water and even praising or occasionally chastising himself. By 1979, Batyr had gained widespread fame as the Speaking Elephant, with numerous media outlets reporting on his abilities. However, many of these reports contained exaggerations and speculative claims. His case was documented in several books on animal behavior and presented at various scientific conferences. This attention brought an influx of visitors to the zoo and even led to an offer from the Czechoslovak Circus to exchange Batyr for a rare dwarf chimpanzee, which the zoo declined. Dr. A.N. Pogrebnoj-Aleksandroff, a scientist who studied Batyr extensively, described the elephant's speech production. Batyr manipulated his trunk by placing its tip in his mouth, pressing it against his lower jaw, and using his tongue to produce words. At times, he would vocalize softly, often at night, with sounds comparable to ultrasonic frequencies or the faint buzzing of mosquitoes. During speech, only the tip of his trunk was inside his mouth, and he made subtle movements with the finger-like projection at the trunk's tip. Audiovisual recordings of Batyr's vocalizations were made during these studies, some of which were later transferred to Moscow State University for further analysis. Batyr's lexicon consisted of approximately 20 words and phrases in Russian and Kazakh, as well as imitations of animal sounds. His repertoire included words like Batyr, I'm Batyr, Water, Good, Bad, and even some human slang, such as an obscene Russian phrase equivalent to fuck you. He also mimicked sounds such as human whistling, the squeaks of rats or mice, the barking of dogs, and the natural calls of elephants. Notably, he could produce sounds at infrasonic and ultrasonic frequencies. Batyr's abilities were reported in various media outlets, including a 1980 article in The Daily Telegraph, which described his capacity to say phrases like Batyr is good and verbs like drink and give. The article also mentioned that his vocalizations were first noticed by a night watchman who heard the elephant talking to himself. Batyr's phenomenon was discussed at several scientific conferences, including events in Kazakhstan, Russia, Estonia, and Ukraine between 1983 and 1990. His case was also featured in books such as The Most Truthful History or Who Are Talking? An Elephant?. by A.N. Pogrebnoj-Aleksandroff and Speaking Animals by A. Dubrov. In addition to scientific documentation, Batyr's story was captured in a student documentary titled Who Speaks? The Elephant… and in audio recordings made by Dr. Pogrebnoj-Aleksandroff between 1979 and 1983. Batyr's death in 1993 was attributed to urological issues, including kidney stones and kidney inflammation.
